body_markdown:
Sir Patrick Stewart enjoyed a career on stage and screen that spanned more than 60 years. He fell in love with Shakespeare as a boy in Mirfield, West Yorkshire, before coming to prominence in the theater, where he was a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company from 1966 until 1982. Spots in British TV shows and TV movies followed, and he landed the role of Gurney Halleck in David Lynch’s adaptation of *Dune* in 1984.


He is of course best known for his role as the deeply intellectual[Captain Jean-Luc Picard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/rating-the-star-trek-captains-by-their-cars/) on *Star Trek: The Next Generation* , which ran from 1987 to 1994, with reprisals in four feature films as well as a later series, *Star Trek: Picard* , which aired from 2020 to 2023. *X-Men* fans, many of whom are probably also *TNG* fans, no doubt remember him as the human mutant Professor Charles Xavier, a role he carried through seven films, from 2000 to 2017.


Stewart, who died October 28 at the age of 86, was also a car guy.


In 1970, Stewart starred as Launce in the Royal Shakespeare Company’s production of *The Two Gentlemen of Verona* , with a rescue dog named Blackie cast for the role of Crab.


Getty Images


Stewart with his Star Trek castmates, including his Prelude pal, Wil Wheaton (back right).


Getty Images


Stewart flanked by X-Men co-stars Hugh Jackman and Ian McKellen.


Flickr/Gage Skidmore


He grew up without a car, but in 1962, aged 22, the self-described lifelong motor racing fan learned to drive in a 1939 Ford. Two years later, he was driving an MG TF. It was then, while co-starring in a playin Bristol with the actress Jane Asher, who was dating Paul McCartney at the time, that the rock star tossed Stewart the keys to[his Aston Martin](https://cars.bonhams.com/auction/24124/lot/132/first-owned-by-sir-paul-mccartney-1964-aston-martin-db5-42-litre-sports-saloon-chassis-no-db51653r/#photos) and asked him to drive the couple from Bristol to Bath, a 15-mile trip. In a 2017 interview with *[The Times](https://www.thetimes.com/culture/music/article/me-and-my-motor-actor-patrick-stewart-pdzvgc2g3?eafs_enabled=false)* of London, Stewart said, “I really didn’t want to be the one responsible for killing a pop star. Paul persuaded me. He sat in the back seat making out with Jane as I drove.”


Stewart married his first wife in 1966 and the couple had two children, and he understood the MG had to go. “I had to buy a rather dull Ford estate,” he told *The Times* . “In the 1970s, there weren’t many exciting cars for a family man with a modest income.”


Although he had no interest in sci-fi and was certain *TNG* was going to be a flop, the show changed Stewart’s fortunes considerably. Perhaps because he’d grown up in poverty, he kept his head and purchased a 1989 Honda Prelude Si, a fun but practical choice. His 16-year-old co-star, Wil Wheaton,[proudly bested him](https://wilwheaton.net/2010/01/from-the-vault-still-cool/) by getting a Prelude Si 4WS…


Courtesy Painting Classic Cars


Courtesy Painting Classic Cars


Courtesy Painting Classic Cars


When the show was picked up for a second season, he added a 1988 Mercedes 420 SEC and then a 1200-mile 1989 Jaguar XJS convertible in British Racing Green, a car Stewart would cherish for decades and[delighted in driving](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CiCz1tvrsMk) . “When I moved back to England after *Star Trek* ,” Stewart told *The Times* , I couldn’t bear to leave it behind.” The Jag remained at his house in the Cotswolds and in 2017 underwent a recommissioning by specialists XjRestorations Ltd. with a respray by[Painting Classic Cars](https://www.paintingclassiccars.co.uk/case-study/sir-patrick-stewarts-jaguar-xjs) . More recently, he drove a Porsche Panamera 4-E Hybrid.


In addition to Stewart’s many acting roles, he also lent his unmistakable, commanding baritone voice to several others, including, er, Poop in *The Emoji Movie* . Long before that, in the early 1990s, he narrated a handful of Pontiac commercials, including one that aired January 28, 1990, during Super Bowl XXIV, and introduced the Trans Sport.


More importantly—in hindsight, perhaps most importantly—were the ads he voiced in the middle of the decade for Porsche. The German carmaker had enjoyed great success in North America throughout the 1980s, with[sales peaking](https://newsroom.porsche.com/en_US/company/porsche-cars-north-america-sales-statistics-18190.html) at more than 30,000 by 1986. By 1993, however, the number had plummeted to 3713, due in no small part to a rise in cost consciousness that overtook the excess and image consciousness of the 1980s.


With a new generation of 911 on the horizon (the 993) and a perception problem to overcome, Porsche dropped its longstanding ad agency, Fallon McElligott, and brought in Goodby Silverstein & Partners (GSP), whose most prominent work to date had been the playful and hugely successful *Got Milk?* campaign of 1993. Porsche, too, wanted playful. And it needed success. With the classically trained, Grammy-winning, Laurence Olivier Award–winning Stewart providing cover for the on-screen visuals, that’s exactly what Porsche got.


“People who didn’t buy \[Porsches\] had certain reactions to people who did,” said GSP principal Jeff Goodby in a 1994 *New York Times* story announcing the new, $20 million campaign, which also included print ads. “So it’s obvious what had to happen: The car had to be taken out of the realm of something that had an off-putting aura and back to being something that worked and performed well, the best thing of its kind, like a Montblanc pen.”


These were Porsche’s first television ads since 1989, and, with Patrick Stewart unseen but at the helm, they worked. A reduction in 911 pricing for 1995 helped, too. North American sales continued to climb for the rest of the decade, hitting 18,207 in 1998, the final model year for the 993.


The campaign included a couple of longer, more cerebral pieces as well, like brief mini-documentaries—one extolling[the virtues of the 993](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H8Vkj5gCikM) and another, entitled “Love Story,” to[introduce the Boxster](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pGTv7lMY9XA) . Stewart’s final Porsche installment came in 1999, an unveiling of the water-cooled 996, from the company that was “not very good at being satisfied.”


All the ads are on YouTube and worth seeking out. In fact, much of Patrick Stewart’s work is worth your attention. He was a serious actor with a deep respect for what he did and how he did it, who later came to understand he could also have some fun while he was at it.


Along the way, he learned to love cars, too.
